params.why: keep the exact answer away from a rounding boundary, so a solver who keeps three decimals in the sine still lands on the same one-decimal answer
using cosine instead of sine must not give the same answer

stem: One of the angles of a rhombus with perimeter ${=4 * s}$ cm is ${=t}^\circ$. Calculate the perpendicular distance between two opposite sides of the rhombus, correct to one decimal place. Do not round off before your final answer.
solution: All four sides of a rhombus are equal, so each side is $\frac{{=4 * s}}{4} = {=s}$ cm.

Call the rhombus $ABCD$ with $\hat{A} = {=t}^\circ$. Draw the perpendicular $DE$ from $D$ to the side $AB$. Then $DE = h$ is the perpendicular distance between the opposite sides $AB$ and $DC$, and triangle $ADE$ is right-angled at $E$ with hypotenuse $AD = {=s}$ cm.
$h$ is opposite the angle ${=t}^\circ$ and we know the hypotenuse, so we use sine: $\sin {=t}^\circ = \frac{h}{{=s}}$.
The perpendicular distance between two opposite sides of the rhombus is about ${=fixed(h, 1)}$ cm.
notes: Advanced: perimeter -> side (all sides equal), then the book's parallelogram-height step (ex11-2-14: h = side * sin of the angle), the same two ideas as ex11-2-15a and ex11-2-14 chained. The angle is acute (25 to 75), so the foot of the perpendicular falls on the side AB itself; every altitude of a rhombus has the same length, so it does not matter which pair of opposite sides the solver picks. Answer = (P/4) * sin t, to one decimal place. The sine table is sin(n degrees) * 10^10 as whole numbers, list index = degrees (0 to 90); cos t is read as sin(90 - t) for the 'wrong ratio' require. Requires keep the exact answer at least 0.025 from a rounding boundary and make using cosine instead of sine give a different answer. Numeric family, no distractors.
